idiom_name: one opaque stage struct per step + functions returning the next stage
implementation_notes: C has no type-level staging, so the classic structure is hand-written: one struct type per step (usually opaque, defined in the .c file), free functions that take the previous stage and return the next one, and a single product type whose only producer is the terminal function. Because the stage types are incompatible, passing an earlier stage where a later one is expected is a constraint violation the compiler reports, and calling the terminal function on a non-terminal stage simply has no matching prototype. The builder state travels in the stage struct so no per-step allocation is needed unless the state must outlive the call chain; when there are fewer than three steps or no ordering rule, one init function taking a fully populated config struct is the simpler form.
pitfalls: Returning the implementation struct instead of the opaque stage type (or defining the stages in the header) lets a caller hand any stage to any function, and the ordering guarantee disappears.
Stage structs returned by pointer need an owner: allocate them in the builder and free them in the terminal function, otherwise every successful build leaks the intermediate states.
There is no compile-time check on the contents of a stage, only on its type: NULL pointers and empty strings still pass the staging and must be validated in dbconfig_build().
sources: ISO/IEC 9899:2018 (C17), 6.7.2.1 'Structure and union specifiers' - the language rules behind distinct stage types and the incomplete-type product.
